newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Giant SAB in spat with tiny Namibian brewer.
newsitem.headline: Giant SAB in spat with tiny Namibian brewer.

text.p: South African Breweries Ltd (SAB), the world's fourth largest brewer, appears to be engaging in a David-and-Goliath battle with a tiny rival from neighbouring Namibia over whose brewing methods are the best.

But unlike the biblical story, there might not be any winners in this contest between SAB and Namibia Breweries (NamBrew) which has been waged for several months through advertising campaigns and the press.

Analysts said NamBrew, which has been brewing beer for the past 75 years in the former German colony with a population of just 1.5 million, has little hope of making inroads into SAB's massive 97 percent dominance of its home market.
Although the Namibian brewer's exports to South Africa are likely to increase it will remain a niche player, they said, estimating its current market share at less than one percent.

The tussle centres on NamBrew priding itself on its beers being brewed according to an ancient Bavarian purity law of 1516 which demands a natural slow fermentation process and the use of malt instead of any other starch.

According to SAB, NamBrew has over the past two years created a perception in the marketplace that beer not brewed according to this Reinheitsgebot -- which includes all SAB's labels -- is inferior. Non-purity law brews are also accused of adding chemicals to speed up the brewing process.

"The impression they are creating is that beer brewed according to the Reinheitsgebot is the only type of beer to drink and the rest is bad," Adrian Botha, public relations manager of SAB's beer division, told Reuters on Wednesday.

The latest salvo has been fired by NamBrew which this week was successful in getting South Africa's Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) to order SAB to withdraw an advertisement for its flagship brand, Castle Lager.
Deline Beukes of the ASA told Reuters SAB was asked to withdraw the advertisement, peppered with superlatives about Castle's ingredients and SAB's achievements, as it was not entirely accurate.
"The campaign as a whole is not in dispute but there is detail that the ASA felt, in view of the consumers lack of knowledge, should be more accurately portrayed," Beukes said.

But SAB said it was a case of sour grapes as NamBrew was last month ordered by the ASA, after a complaint by SAB, to withdraw its entire advertising campaign which according to the ASA "presented a disparaging picture of their competitor SAB".
"It is a tit-for-tat response to them having to pull their whole campaign before Christmas," SAB's Botha said.
The ASA's Beukes said NamBrew had appealed against the withdrawal of their campaign although all "offending" advertisements were being removed before the result of the appeal in late January.
NamBrew was not immediately available for comment.
Botha downplayed talk of a war between the two rivals saying SAB's advertising campaign was not aimed at NamBrew but was an attempt to protect the image of beer.

"It is not a war, it is not a battle, it is just a simple thing that we took to try and stop the nastiness about beer...(NamBrew's emphasis on the purity law) has damaged the perception and culture of beer," he said, adding that sales of Castle were continuing to grow.
But other facts, including SAB's decision earlier this year to sell its five percent stake in its upstart competitor, point to the contrary.

SAB, which controls around 10 percent of the Namibian market, is keen to expand and has accused NamBrew of protectionism. NamBrew has responded by questioning SAB's reasons for wanting to open a brewery given the small market.
Outside South Africa SAB is the largest brewer in Poland, Hungary and Romania and has interests in other parts of southern Africa and China.
The SAB group, which has holdings in a number of industrial companies, last month reported half year earnings up over 16 percent to 553 million rand on turnover of 17.16 billion rand.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
